rw: The earlier you start, the longer your returns earn their own returns, so even small regular deposits can grow into a much larger balance over decades.

ww.Early investors never lose any money: Investing always carries some risk of loss, and starting early does not remove it; it only gives more years to recover from market downturns.
ww.Taxes vanish for early investors: Taxes do not disappear for anyone; early investors still owe taxes on gains, though accounts like a Roth IRA or 401(k) can defer or reduce them.
ww.Fees are lower for early investors: Fund fees depend on the product chosen, such as expense ratios, not on when you begin; starting early does not make fees any lower for you.

rw: A REIT is a company that owns or finances income-producing property such as offices or apartments, and it must pay most of its income to shareholders as dividends.

ww.A property tax paid by owners of real es: Property tax is a levy local governments charge real estate owners each year; a REIT is an investment company, not a tax owed on property.
ww.A mortgage for a home that a family buys: A mortgage is a loan used to buy a home, repaid to a lender; a REIT is a company that investors buy shares in, not a loan.
ww.A homeowners policy that covers fire dam: Homeowners insurance is a policy covering fire and theft damage to a house and its contents; a REIT is an investment company, not a form of insurance.

rw: REITs let investors own real estate without buying buildings directly, spreading portfolio risk across asset types while paying regular dividend income that must be distributed from rents and property profits.

ww.To avoid all risk in the whole portfolio: No investment removes all risk, and REIT shares can fall in price with real estate markets and interest rates, so this would not eliminate portfolio risk.
ww.To guarantee profit every year, as real: REITs offer no guaranteed profit; rents, property values and share prices can all fall, and returns vary from year to year like other stocks.
ww.To avoid all taxes on the income it pays: REIT dividends are generally taxable income to the shareholder, often taxed at ordinary rates, so a REIT does not let you avoid taxes on what it pays.

rw: Penny stocks generally trade for under five dollars, often on small over-the-counter markets, with little public information and thin trading, which makes them prone to sharp swings and manipulation.

ww.A stock issued only to children who cann: Penny stocks are not a children's product; anyone with a brokerage account can buy them, and the name refers to their very low share price instead.
ww.A government bond that pays a fixed rate: A government bond is a debt security paying fixed interest, such as a Treasury; a penny stock is an equity share in a small company.
ww.A stock worth one cent forever and never: Penny stock prices move up and down like any stock; the name only describes a low price, and the price is never fixed at one cent.

rw: Urgent hype about a cheap stock is a warning sign of a pump-and-dump scheme, so verify the company with SEC filings and independent research before putting any money in.

ww.Send your password to claim your free sh: Sending your password to a stranger is a classic scam; no legitimate offer requires your login, and doing so gives criminals access to your accounts.
ww.Share it with all friends right away: Passing along an unverified tip can spread a pump-and-dump scheme, where promoters inflate a price and sell, leaving others holding losses; it also may expose you legally.
ww.Invest everything immediately on the tip: Investing everything on one social media tip ignores diversification and due diligence, and penny stocks are often manipulated, so you could lose your entire stake quickly.

rw: Employees have tax withheld from each paycheck, but self-employed people have no employer doing this, so they pay estimated tax quarterly to the IRS to cover income and self-employment taxes.

ww.Estimated taxes are optional for everyon: Estimated taxes are required for those expected to owe about $1,000 or more after withholding and credits; skipping them can bring underpayment penalties.
ww.Self-employed people are exempt from pay: Self-employed people are not exempt; they owe income tax plus self-employment tax for Social Security and Medicare on their net earnings every year.
ww.Estimated taxes replace the need to file: Estimated payments are only advance payments toward the bill; the self-employed still must file an annual return, typically with Schedule C, to report income and reconcile.

rw: With no employer withholding, the tutor should keep records of income and expenses and set aside part of each payment, since taxes will be due and estimated payments may be required.

ww.Hide the income so that no one ever know: Hiding income is tax evasion, which is illegal and can bring penalties and interest; all income must be reported whether or not a pay stub exists.
ww.Nothing, because tutoring is never taxed: Tutoring income is taxable as self-employment income, and net earnings of $400 or more in a year require reporting and self-employment tax, so doing nothing is wrong.
ww.Wait for the students to pay the tax for: Students who pay for tutoring are not responsible for the tutor's income tax; the tutor, as the earner, must report the income and pay the tax.

rw: A probationary period, often 30 to 90 days, lets an employer evaluate a new hire's performance and fit, and it may be easier to end employment during this time.

ww.A period when the employee is not paid f: Probationary employees are paid for their work under wage laws; the period is about evaluation, not unpaid service, and unpaid work would break minimum wage rules.
ww.A paid vacation for new hires in their f: A paid first week of vacation is not what probation means; new hires usually earn vacation later, and the period is about evaluating performance instead.
ww.A period when the employee cannot be rev: Employees on probation are typically reviewed more closely, not less, so a boss being unable to review them is the opposite of what the period involves.

rw: Job security is how likely someone is to stay employed; it is higher in stable industries and roles, with steady demand and contracts, than in seasonal or declining ones.

ww.A guard who protects an office and check: A security guard protects a building and checks badges, which is physical security for property; job security is about a worker's employment, not about the workplace.
ww.A password for work computers and email: A password protects work accounts and is called information security; job security is about whether your employment continues and has nothing to do with login credentials.
ww.A list of job openings at a firm or a co: A list of openings is a job board or posting; job security concerns whether you are likely to keep your current job, not what positions exist.

rw: A salary pays a set amount on a regular schedule, which makes budgeting easier, while seasonal freelance income swings with demand and can disappear for part of the year.

ww.They are identical: The two are not identical; a salaried job pays a fixed amount each pay period, while seasonal freelance work varies with demand and may stop for months.
ww.Seasonal freelance work: Seasonal freelance work pays only during busy periods and can leave gaps with no income, so it is less steady than a salaried office job.
ww.Neither earns income: Both kinds of work earn income; the question is which is steadier, and a salaried position is more predictable than seasonal freelance gigs.

rw: A pay stub lists gross pay and each deduction, such as taxes and insurance, so you can see how it becomes the net pay deposited into your account.

ww.Filing your taxes for you each year: A pay stub does not file taxes; it shows earnings and deductions, and you use that information, along with your W-2, when you prepare a return yourself.
ww.Requesting a raise from your boss now: A pay stub is a record of your pay, not a request form; asking for a raise is done by talking with your employer or manager.
ww.Applying for a loan automatically: Pay stubs cannot apply for loans; they can serve as proof of income when you apply, but you must submit the application to a lender yourself.

rw: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions, so $900 - $135 taxes - $45 insurance = $720, which is the amount actually received in your paycheck.

ww.$1,080: $1,080 is wrong because it subtracts nothing close to the deductions; $900 minus $180 would give $720, so adding $180 to gross is a mistake.
ww.$180: $180 is the total of deductions, $135 + $45; it is the amount taken out, not the take-home pay left after subtracting it from gross pay.
ww.$765: $765 results from subtracting only the $135 in taxes ($900 - $135) and forgetting the $45 insurance deduction, so the net pay is overstated.

rw: Waiting a few days or weeks helps you tell a lasting need from an impulse, and it gives time to compare prices and save, which prevents regret.

ww.You will forget about your real needs la: Waiting does not make you forget what you really need; if the item matters, you will still want it later, and the pause only filters out impulse buys.
ww.Prices never change at any time of the y: Prices change often because of sales, seasons and new models, so claiming they never change is false, and waiting can even let you catch a discount.
ww.Waiting always makes the item cheaper to: Waiting does not always lower the price; items can rise in cost or sell out, though it may let you find a sale or a better alternative.

rw: When both meet your needs, the refurbished phone at $420 saves $180 ($600 - $420) and the warranty covers repairs, so it gives more value per dollar spent.

ww.The most expensive one: The most expensive option is not automatically the best value; if both phones meet your needs, paying $180 more for the same use gives no extra benefit.
ww.Neither, they are equal: The two are not equal, since one costs $600 and the other $420; the refurbished phone saves $180 while its warranty protects against defects.
ww.The newest phone model: The newest model is the $600 one here, and its higher price buys features you do not need, so it is the poorer value for the same use.

rw: A rebate is a partial refund of the purchase price, usually claimed after the sale by mail or online with a receipt, and some buyers forget to claim it.

ww.A coupon used before you buy at the till: A coupon is redeemed at purchase to cut the price immediately, whereas a rebate gives money back after you buy and send in proof of purchase.
ww.A fee charged at checkout by the store: A fee charged at checkout adds to your cost, while a rebate returns money to you; the two work in opposite directions.
ww.A tax on a purchase made at a retail sto: A sales tax is a government charge added to purchases; a rebate is a refund of part of the price offered by a maker or store.

rw: The rebate returns part of the price, so $200 - $30 = $170, assuming you send in the claim on time and in the right form.

ww.$30: $30 is only the rebate amount, not the final cost; you must subtract it from the $200 price to find what you actually paid.
ww.$230: $230 adds the rebate to the price instead of subtracting it; a rebate returns money to you, so it lowers the cost rather than raising it.
ww.$200: $200 is the price before the rebate; if you claim the $30 mail-in rebate, your final cost drops by that amount, to $170.

rw: Reviews reveal how real buyers found quality, durability and problems, which helps you spot weaknesses before spending, especially when many detailed reviews agree on the same points.

ww.They guarantee your full satisfaction: No review guarantees satisfaction; reviews are other people's opinions, and a product can still disappoint you, though they reduce the chance of a bad buy.
ww.They remove the need to compare options: Reviews are one input to comparing options, not a replacement; you still compare features, prices and warranties across several products before deciding.
ww.They set the price of the item you buy: Sellers and markets set prices, not reviewers; reviews describe quality and experience, though a well-reviewed product may help justify a price you see.

rw: A detailed review gives specifics about quality, performance and flaws, so you can judge whether the product fits your needs and spot patterns across many reviews.

ww.A review that says Worst ever, with no r: A bare complaint with no reasons gives you no facts to evaluate; it could reflect shipping trouble or a personal gripe unrelated to product quality.
ww.A review that says Great!!! and nothing: An enthusiastic review with no details tells you nothing about what the buyer liked, and such posts can be fake or paid, so it is little help.
ww.A review with no text at all, only a sta: A star rating alone shows overall satisfaction but not why, so you cannot tell whether low scores came from the product or from other issues.

rw: A refund returns money to a buyer when a purchase is returned or cancelled, and stores' return policies set time limits and conditions for getting one.

ww.Extra pay for overtime, added to a paych: Overtime pay is extra wages for hours beyond forty in a week under federal law, paid to workers; a refund is money returned to a buyer.
ww.A discount before a sale starts, offered: A pre-sale member discount lowers the price you pay up front; a refund returns money after a purchase has already been paid for.
ww.A tax paid at checkout on the items that: Sales tax is a government charge added at checkout, which you pay on top of the price; a refund returns money instead of collecting it.

rw: APY, or annual percentage yield, is the real yearly return including compounding, so it lets you compare accounts fairly even if they compound at different frequencies.

ww.The minimum balance required by the bank: A minimum balance is a required amount the account must hold to avoid fees; APY measures the interest you earn, not a balance requirement.
ww.The yearly fee for owning the account it: A yearly fee is an annual maintenance charge that reduces your money; APY is the interest you earn, expressed as a yearly percentage.
ww.The monthly deposit amount you must make: A required monthly deposit is a bank rule for certain accounts; APY describes the interest return, not any deposit that you must make.

rw: $1,000 x 3.0% = $30 and $1,000 x 2.2% = $22, so Account A earns $30 - $22 = $8 more over the year.

ww.$0.80: $0.80 is off by a factor of ten; the rate gap is 0.8 percentage points, and 0.8% of $1,000 is $8, not $0.80.
ww.$52: $52 adds the two earnings, $30 + $22, instead of subtracting them; the question asks how much more A earns than B, which is the difference.
ww.$80: $80 mistakes the 0.8 percentage point gap for 8%; the correct figure is $1,000 x 0.008 = $8, not $80.

rw: A money market account is an insured deposit account that often pays higher interest than regular savings, but it may limit withdrawals or transactions and require a higher balance.

ww.A loan for a car that is repaid in fixed: That describes an auto loan, which is debt repaid monthly with interest; a money market account is a deposit account where you earn interest, not borrow.
ww.A retirement plan that employers offer a: That describes an employer retirement plan such as a 401(k); a money market account is a bank deposit account that you open yourself for savings.
ww.A stock account for buying shares in pub: That describes a brokerage account for buying shares; money market accounts hold insured deposits at banks and carry low risk instead of the high risk of stocks.

rw: With the balance often under $500, the $10 fee applies each month, so $10 x 12 months = $120 per year in fees.

ww.$30: $30 is only three months of the $10 fee; the question asks for the full year, which covers twelve months of charges.
ww.$10: $10 is the monthly charge, not the yearly total; multiplying by the 12 months of the year gives the amount the question asks for.
ww.$500: $500 is the minimum balance required to avoid the fee, not the fee itself; the fee is $10 a month, which is $120 over a year.

rw: An overdraft happens when you spend more than your checking balance; the bank may cover it but often charges a fee, or may decline the payment.

ww.Closing an account at the bank for good: Closing an account is a decision made by the customer or bank; an overdraft is a negative balance caused by spending more than is available.
ww.Earning interest on a balance, which the: Earning interest on a balance is a gain, not a shortfall; an overdraft is the opposite, where the account goes below zero and costs you money.
ww.Depositing more than needed into a savin: Depositing extra funds into savings is a smart habit that adds money; an overdraft happens when too much is taken out of checking.

rw: Knowing your balance and setting low-balance alerts warns you before an account runs short, and linking savings for overdraft protection can also help avoid fees.

ww.Spending first and checking your balance: Spending first and checking later is how overdrafts happen, since a purchase can exceed your balance before you notice, which triggers a fee.
ww.Ignoring your balance and all of your ac: Ignoring alerts removes your early warning; alerts tell you when the balance is low, so skipping them makes an overdraft more likely.
ww.Using several cards without tracking any: Using several cards without tracking balances makes it easy to lose sight of spending and money available, so overdrafts and debts become more likely.

rw: Direct deposit electronically sends your pay from the employer straight into your bank account, which is fast, safe from loss and often available on payday.

ww.Handing out cash to staff every week: Handing out cash is a manual payment method, not direct deposit; direct deposit moves pay electronically into a bank account without cash or paper.
ww.Mailing a paper check to be deposited la: Mailing a paper check requires depositing it yourself later; direct deposit sends the pay electronically so no paper check is involved or delayed.
ww.Paying wages in goods rather than in mon: Paying in goods is bartering, not direct deposit; direct deposit is a way of paying wages in money through the banking system.

rw: A credit inquiry occurs when a lender or other party requests your credit report; hard inquiries come from applications and can slightly lower your score.

ww.A bill for credit sent to you by a store: A bill for credit is a statement of what you owe; an inquiry is when someone checks your credit file, not a bill sent to you.
ww.A payment reminder sent by the lender's: A payment reminder is a notice about a due date; a credit inquiry is a check of your credit report by an authorized party.
ww.A request to cancel a card, made by a ca: Cancelling a card is an account action you take with the issuer; a credit inquiry is a lender looking at your credit report.

rw: Each application usually triggers a hard inquiry, and many in a short span can signal risk to lenders, which may lower your score and reduce approval odds.

ww.The cards cancel your inquiries, so your: Inquiries do not cancel each other out; each application can add a hard inquiry, and several in a short time can still lower your score.
ww.Your score will rise sharply within a mo: Multiple applications do not raise a score sharply; new credit requests tend to lower it, and a sudden rise from this behavior would be unusual.
ww.Nothing will happen to your credit score: Hard inquiries can affect a score, usually by a few points each, so the claim that nothing happens is wrong, particularly when several occur together.

rw: Payment history is the largest factor in a credit score, and a late payment reported to the bureaus can hurt your score and remain on your report for up to seven years.

ww.It has no effect on your credit score or: Payments 30 or more days late are reported to the credit bureaus, and payment history is the biggest score factor, so the effect is not zero.
ww.It raises your score by a set number of: Late payments do not add points; they hurt scores, and a clean record over time is what helps a score recover, not lateness.
ww.It deletes your debt from the books of t: A late payment does not erase debt; you still owe the balance, and the lender may add late fees and penalty interest on top.

rw: Automatic payments or calendar reminders make sure the bill is paid before the 5th, avoiding late fees, interest penalties and the damage a late payment does to your credit.

ww.Paying after the due date has already pa: Paying after the due date means the payment is late, which can bring a fee, a higher rate, and a mark on your credit report.
ww.Paying whenever you remember, as lenders: Lenders do not simply wait; they charge late fees and report delinquencies, so paying whenever you remember risks fees and credit score damage.
ww.Ignoring statements that arrive in the m: Ignoring statements causes missed due dates and errors to go unnoticed, which leads to late fees and damaged credit instead of preventing them.

rw: An annual fee is a yearly charge for keeping the card, usually on rewards or premium cards, and it is worth paying only if the benefits you use exceed it.

ww.A fee for paying a bill very late: A late fee is charged when you miss a due date; an annual fee is charged once a year just for having the card open.
ww.A reward for using the card each month: An annual fee is a cost to you, not a reward; rewards like cash back are separate perks that the fee may or may not be worth.
ww.A fee for each purchase that you make: A fee for each purchase would be a transaction fee; an annual fee is charged one time per year no matter how many purchases you make.

rw: Rewards of $120 minus the $95 fee leave a net gain of $25 each year, so the card is worth keeping if you would use those rewards.

ww.It cannot be told: You can tell using the numbers given: $120 in rewards less the $95 fee equals a $25 gain, so the answer is clear.
ww.No, it loses $25: A loss of $25 reverses the subtraction; rewards of $120 exceed the $95 fee, which produces a $25 gain rather than a loss.
ww.No, it loses $215: $215 adds the fee and the rewards ($95 + $120) instead of comparing them; the net result is the difference, which is a $25 gain.

rw: An introductory APR is a low or 0% rate offered for a limited time, often 6 to 18 months, after which the regular, higher rate applies to balances.

ww.A rate that applies only to cash advance: Cash advance rates are a separate APR usually higher than the purchase rate; an introductory APR is a temporary rate for new purchases or transfers.
ww.A permanent low rate that never changes: Introductory rates are temporary by definition; a low rate that never changes would be a permanent rate, and cards do not promise that.
ww.A fee for opening a card, paid to the is: A fee for opening a card would be an account opening or annual fee; an introductory APR is an interest rate, not a fee.

rw: You need to know when the promotional period ends and what regular APR then applies, so you can plan to pay off the balance before higher interest starts.

ww.Only the color of the card and its logo: The card color and logo have no effect on your cost; the real terms are in the offer, including the length of the intro period and later rates.
ww.Nothing, because 0% is permanent and nev: Introductory 0% rates are temporary, and when they end the regular APR applies to any balance left, which is why you should not assume it lasts.
ww.Only the name of the issuer printed on t: The issuer's name tells you little about the cost of the offer; the key facts are the promotional length, balance transfer fees and the regular APR.

rw: Most health plans reset the deductible at the start of each plan year, often January 1, so what you paid last year does not carry over.

ww.Never, it is a fixed amount: Deductibles are not fixed forever; most health plans reset them, so you pay your share again each plan year before the insurer starts paying.
ww.Every month of each year: Deductibles generally reset yearly on the plan year, not monthly; you pay the deductible once per year and not every 30 days.
ww.Each time you visit a doctor: A doctor visit does not reset the deductible; it counts toward it, and the amount continues to accumulate across visits within the plan year.

rw: A healthy young adult uses little care, so low premiums save money, and an HSA lets them save pre-tax dollars for costs that may arise.

ww.It pays for everything with no cost to t: High-deductible plans do not pay everything; you pay the deductible and sometimes coinsurance before the plan pays, so costs for patients can be significant.
ww.It never denies claims of any kind from: No plan pays every claim; insurers can deny claims that are not covered or lack medical necessity, and high-deductible plans are no exception.
ww.It has no deductible and no out-of-pocke: High-deductible plans are named for their large deductible, and out-of-pocket costs apply up to a yearly maximum, so costs are not zero.

rw: A generic has the same active ingredient, strength and use as the brand-name drug, but it costs less because makers avoid the original research and marketing costs.

ww.A medicine that is always unsafe to take: Generic drugs are approved by the FDA as safe and effective when taken as directed; they are not inherently unsafe at all.
ww.A medicine with no active ingredient, so: Generics must contain the same active ingredient as the brand drug, so a medicine with none would not be a generic; the lower price comes from lower marketing costs.
ww.A medicine only for pets, made by vets a: Generic drugs are for people and approved by the FDA; veterinary medicines are a separate category, so this does not describe generics.

rw: Preventive care, such as vaccines, screenings and annual checkups, aims to stop illness or catch it early, and many plans cover it at no cost to you.

ww.Treatment after a serious injury, in a h: Emergency room treatment is care after an injury or sudden illness has already happened, so it is not preventive; prevention comes before a problem arises.
ww.A tax on health services that patients m: Preventive care is a service, not a tax; patients are not charged a tax on health services at each doctor visit.
ww.A fee for visiting a specialist that is: A specialist visit fee is a copay for treatment of a condition; preventive care is routine services meant to prevent illness and is often covered fully.

rw: Finding conditions early, such as high blood pressure or cancer, lets treatment start sooner when it is simpler and cheaper than treating advanced disease later.

ww.It makes premiums zero for everyone who: Preventive care does not make premiums zero; premiums are set by plans and risk, and checkups may lower costs later but not erase the premium.
ww.It is always free everywhere in the whol: Preventive care is not free everywhere; many insurance plans cover it, but uninsured people or those using out-of-network providers may still pay.
ww.It removes all medical risk for every pe: Checkups reduce risk but cannot remove it; people can still become ill or injured, so insurance remains necessary even with preventive care.

rw: The policyholder owns the policy, pays the premiums, and holds the contract rights, and may be a different person from the insured or the beneficiary.

ww.The company that issues the policy each: The company that issues the policy is the insurer, not the policyholder; the policyholder is the customer who buys and owns the coverage.
ww.A person who files a lawsuit in court: A person who files a lawsuit is a plaintiff in a court case; a policyholder is the owner of an insurance policy.
ww.A person who sells policies for a firm: A person who sells policies is an insurance agent or broker; the policyholder is the buyer who owns the coverage and pays premiums.

rw: A beneficiary is named to receive proceeds from a life insurance policy or retirement account when the owner dies, and the named person gets it without probate in most cases.

ww.The person who pays the premium on an in: The person who pays premiums is the policyholder or owner; a beneficiary is the person named to receive the benefit when a claim is paid.
ww.The person who sells the policy to the o: The person who sells a policy is an agent or broker; a beneficiary is someone who receives the payout and has no role in the sale.
ww.The company that insures the person and: The company that insures you and pays claims is the insurer; a beneficiary is a person or entity named to receive the proceeds.

rw: After marriage, divorce, birth or death in the family, outdated beneficiary forms could send money to an ex-spouse or the wrong person, so updating them matches your wishes.

ww.Because beneficiaries pay your premiums: Beneficiaries do not pay premiums; the policyholder pays them, and a beneficiary only receives the proceeds if the owner dies.
ww.Because insurers require yearly changes: Insurers do not require yearly changes; you review beneficiaries on your own after events such as marriage, divorce or a birth.
ww.Because beneficiaries never matter: Beneficiaries matter a great deal because the form usually overrides a will, so the named person gets the money, which is why you keep it current.

rw: A collision or loss damage waiver is optional coverage in which the rental company agrees not to charge you for damage or theft of the car, though your own policy may already cover this.

ww.A discount on gas for the rental car you: A gas discount is a fuel pricing offer; a rental car waiver relates to damage liability and does not change fuel costs.
ww.A tax on car rentals that the state char: A tax on car rentals is a government surcharge added to the bill; the waiver is optional coverage you can accept or decline.
ww.A fee for returning a car late to the re: A late return fee is a penalty for missing the return time; the waiver is a damage coverage option and has nothing to do with timing.

rw: A prospectus is the formal document an investment company must provide, describing goals, strategy, fees, risks and past performance so you can decide before investing.

ww.A tax return filed by a person with the: A tax return is filed with the IRS to report income; a prospectus is an investment disclosure document, not a tax filing.
ww.A bank statement showing the deposits an: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals on your account; a prospectus describes an investment product you might buy instead.
ww.A list of broker employees with their na: A list of broker employees is not a prospectus; it is a disclosure about an investment's objectives, costs and risks, not about the staff.

rw: The fee and expense table lists the expense ratio, loads and other charges, which lets you compare the yearly cost of owning different funds.

ww.The list of fund staff names: The list of fund staff names tells you who works there but nothing about costs; fees are shown in the fee table, not in a staff list.
ww.The cover photo and title: The cover and title identify the fund but give no cost detail; the comparison data is found inside the document in the fee tables.
ww.The contact page details: Contact details tell you how to reach the fund company but have no cost information, so they are no help in comparing the fees of funds.

rw: Agencies such as Moody's and S&P grade an issuer's ability to repay debt, from AAA at the top to D for default, which helps investors weigh risk.

ww.The number of bonds issued by a firm eac: The number of bonds a firm issues is its issuance volume; a rating measures credit quality, not how many bonds were sold.
ww.The interest rate set by the Fed for ban: The interest rate set by the Fed for bank loans is the federal funds rate; a bond rating assesses a specific issuer's creditworthiness.
ww.The price of a stock on a given day of t: A stock's daily price comes from the market; a bond rating is a credit assessment from agencies like Moody's or S&P.

rw: AAA is the highest credit rating, showing a very strong ability to repay, so it is generally the lowest-risk bond though its yield is usually lower.

ww.A bond rated CCC: CCC is a speculative, low rating signaling high default risk; it is far riskier than AAA, so it is not the lowest-risk choice.
ww.A bond rated D: A D rating means the issuer is already in default, which is the highest risk of all and the opposite of a low-risk bond.
ww.An unrated bond note: An unrated bond has not been assessed by a rating agency, so its credit risk is unknown and generally cannot be called the lowest.

rw: A ticker symbol is a short code, such as AAPL or KO, that identifies a publicly traded company on an exchange for trading and quotes.

ww.A password for a brokerage account login: A password protects a brokerage login; a ticker symbol is a public code that identifies a stock, not a secret used for access.
ww.A tax code used on stock trades by the I: The IRS does not create ticker symbols; stock trades are taxed on gains, but the ticker is a short code assigned by the exchange.
ww.A government license number for a listed: A ticker is not a government license; it is an exchange-assigned code, and companies are listed under exchange rules and SEC registration instead.

rw: Cost basis is what you originally paid for an investment, including fees, and the difference between it and the sale price determines your taxable gain or loss.

ww.The tax paid on gains from a sale of sha: Tax paid on gains is a separate item, the capital gains tax; cost basis is the original purchase price used to calculate the gain.
ww.The fee paid to a broker for each stock: A broker's trade fee is a commission, which may be added to cost basis, but the cost basis itself means the original purchase price.
ww.The price at which the asset is later so: The later sale price is the proceeds; cost basis is the original price paid, and the gain is the sale price minus that basis.

rw: The gain is the sale price minus the cost basis, so $1,400 - $1,000 = $400, which may be subject to capital gains tax.

ww.$1,000: $1,000 is the original cost, not the profit; the gain is how much more you received than you paid, which is $400.
ww.$2,400: $2,400 adds the cost and the sale price together; gain is a difference, so subtract $1,000 from $1,400 to get $400.
ww.$1,400: $1,400 is the sale proceeds in total, which includes getting back your $1,000; only the extra $400 is the gain.

rw: Long-term investing means holding for years, which lets compounding work, lowers trading costs, and may qualify gains for lower long-term capital gains tax rates after one year.

ww.Selling after one week of holding the in: Selling after one week is short-term trading, not long-term investing; a long-term horizon usually means years, often through market ups and downs.
ww.Trading every day to chase small moves i: Trading every day is active trading; it is the opposite of holding long term, which means staying invested and ignoring short-term moves.
ww.Buying only to resell right away for a q: Buying only to resell right away is short-term speculation; a long-term investor buys to hold and benefit from growth and compounding.

rw: Each trade may carry commissions or spreads, and short-term gains are taxed at higher ordinary rates, so frequent trading often leaves less money after costs and taxes.

ww.It eliminates all of your risk: Trading often cannot remove risk; every trade involves market risk, and more trades can add costs and mistakes instead of lowering risk.
ww.It guarantees losses every year: Frequent trading does not guarantee losses; some trades win, but costs and poor timing make it harder to earn good returns over time.
ww.It always raises returns by a lot: Frequent trading seldom raises returns by a lot; studies show active traders often lag buy-and-hold investors once costs and taxes are counted.

rw: A deduction subtracts from your income before the tax is calculated, so a $1,000 deduction at a 22% rate saves about $220 in tax.

ww.An amount that is subtracted from the ta: That describes a tax credit, which is subtracted from the tax itself after it is figured; a deduction reduces the income being taxed.
ww.A refund sent by a bank on request when: A refund is money returned when you overpaid; a deduction is a reduction in taxable income and is not sent by a bank.
ww.An extra penalty added for filing late o: An extra charge for filing late is a penalty; a deduction is a benefit that lowers taxable income and never adds a cost.

rw: A credit is subtracted directly from the tax you owe, so a $500 credit cuts your bill by $500, and refundable credits can even produce a refund.

ww.An amount that lowers taxable income bef: That describes a deduction, which lowers taxable income before the rate applies; a credit instead reduces the tax bill itself after it is calculated.
ww.A fine for underpaying your tax bill in: A fine for underpayment is a penalty; a tax credit is a benefit that reduces your tax, such as the child tax credit.
ww.A loan from the government to help pay y: A government loan to help with taxes is not a credit; a credit is a reduction of tax owed that you do not repay.

rw: The credit cuts tax by the full $500, while the deduction saves only $500 x 12% = $60, so the credit is worth far more.

ww.Neither affects tax: Both deductions and credits do affect tax; a deduction lowers taxable income and a credit lowers the tax itself, so neither is zero.
ww.The $500 deduction: The deduction only reduces taxable income by $500, saving $500 x 0.12 = $60 in tax, which is much less than the $500 credit.
ww.Equal in value: They are not equal: the deduction saves $60 at a 12% rate while the credit saves $500, so the credit is worth more.

rw: The standard deduction is a set amount, based on filing status, that most taxpayers subtract from income without listing expenses, and it is adjusted yearly for inflation.

ww.A deduction that must be itemized by eac: The standard deduction is the alternative to itemizing; taxpayers choose one or the other, so it is not a deduction you itemize.
ww.A deduction only for businesses, claimed: The standard deduction is available to individual filers, not just businesses; it is claimed on a personal return such as Form 1040.
ww.A fee for filing a return that the IRS c: The IRS does not charge a fee for filing; the standard deduction is a benefit that lowers taxable income and does not add costs.

rw: Individual returns are generally due April 15, or the next business day when that date falls on a weekend or holiday; extensions delay filing but not payment.

ww.June 30 of the same year as earned: June 30 is not the deadline for individual federal returns; April 15 is the normal date, and filing after it can bring penalties.
ww.December 31 of the same year earned: December 31 ends the tax year and is not a filing deadline; the return for that year is due the following April.
ww.January 1 of the year that follows: January 1 is the start of a new tax year; returns for the previous year are due in April, after forms like the W-2 arrive.

rw: With $0 withheld, a student may owe nothing or may still need to file, so they should check the IRS filing rules and claim any refund or credits they earn.

ww.Ignore taxes completely and file nothing: Ignoring it is risky; whether a return is needed depends on income and filing status, and filing may be needed or may get a refund.
ww.Let their employer file for them, since: Employers do not file employees' personal returns; they send a W-2 and the employee files their own return or uses a tax service.
ww.Pay a random amount to be safe, with no: Guessing a payment without forms is unreliable; taxes are calculated on a return, and records are needed to support what you report to the IRS.

rw: Gross pay is total earnings before taxes and deductions, while net pay, or take-home pay, is what you actually receive after those amounts come out.

ww.Gross pay is the amount after deductions: This reverses the terms: gross pay is the total earned before deductions, and net pay is what is left after taxes and other deductions.
ww.They are the same amount, just named in: They differ: gross pay is the full amount earned and net pay is the smaller take-home amount after taxes and deductions are subtracted.
ww.Gross pay is only tips; net pay is only: Gross pay includes all earnings such as wages, tips and bonuses before deductions; it is not only tips, and net pay is not only base wage.

rw: Percent deducted = $240 / $1,200 = 0.20, or 20%, meaning the worker takes home the other 80% of gross pay.

ww.24%: 24% is wrong because it likely divides by the wrong base; $240 divided by $1,200 is 0.20, so the correct figure is 20%.
ww.80%: 80% is the share kept as net pay ($960 / $1,200); the question asks for the share deducted, which is the remaining 20%.
ww.5%: 5% would result if you divided by a much larger figure; $240 divided by $1,200 equals 20%, not 5%.

rw: A raise is an increase in pay, either in hourly wage or salary, often given for performance, experience or cost-of-living adjustments.

ww.A decrease in your pay: A decrease in pay is a pay cut; a raise goes the opposite way and means you earn more for the same work.
ww.A tax taken from pay: A tax taken from pay is a withholding or deduction; a raise adds to your pay and is not something that is taken out.
ww.A one-time gift: A one-time gift is a bonus or present; a raise is a lasting increase in your regular pay rate or salary.

rw: A 4% raise is 15 x 0.04 = $0.60, and $15.00 + $0.60 = $15.60 per hour as the new wage.

ww.$19.00: $19.00 adds 4 dollars rather than 4 percent; a 4% raise on $15 is only 60 cents, so the new wage is $15.60.
ww.$16.00: $16.00 adds a full dollar, which would be about a 6.7% raise; 4% of $15 is $0.60, giving $15.60.
ww.$15.04: $15.04 adds only 4 cents, treating the 4% as 0.04 dollars; the raise is 4% of $15, which is 60 cents.

rw: A renter pays a landlord for the right to live in a property, while a buyer owns it, gaining equity and also taking on taxes, repairs and mortgage payments.

ww.Renting means owning; buying means borro: This is backwards: renting means paying to use a place you do not own, and buying a home is usually financed through a mortgage.
ww.Renting is free, while buying costs you: Renting is not free; tenants pay monthly rent, and buying costs money too, including a down payment, mortgage, taxes and upkeep.
ww.They are exactly the same thing in every: Renting and buying differ in ownership, costs, flexibility and responsibility for repairs, so they are not the same in any case.

rw: A landlord usually pays for major repairs like roofs and plumbing, while an owner must pay for them, so renters generally avoid this cost.

ww.Utilities such as power and gas: Renters usually pay utilities such as power and gas, as owners do, so this is a cost both groups share.
ww.Monthly rent paid to the landlord: Renters pay monthly rent to the landlord, while owners make mortgage payments instead, so rent is a cost renters pay.
ww.Renters insurance for belongings: Renters insurance covers a tenant's belongings and is the tenant's responsibility, so it is a cost that renters do pay.

rw: A security deposit is held by the landlord to cover damage beyond normal wear or unpaid rent, and it should be returned if nothing is owed.

ww.A monthly fee for living in a place, pai: Monthly rent is the regular fee for living in the place; a security deposit is a separate one-time amount held against possible damage.
ww.A tax on rentals that the landlord pays: A tax on rentals paid by the landlord is a government charge; a security deposit is paid by the tenant and is refundable if no damage is found.
ww.A gift to the landlord when you move int: A deposit is not a gift; it is money the tenant paid that belongs to the tenant if no damage or unpaid rent is found.

rw: Laws in most states require the landlord to return the deposit within a set period, less deductions for unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear.

ww.It becomes rent for next month and the o: A deposit does not automatically become rent; it is held as security and is returned at the end of the lease if the unit is in good condition.
ww.The tenant owes another $600 for the dam: A tenant who leaves the place in good condition owes nothing extra; additional charges apply only for real damage beyond normal wear.
ww.The landlord keeps it whatever the condi: A landlord cannot keep a deposit regardless of condition; legitimate deductions are limited to damage or unpaid rent, and the rest must be returned.

rw: A lease is a legal contract in which a landlord lets a tenant use property for a set term, such as 12 months, in exchange for rent.

ww.A loan to buy a house, repaid with inter: A mortgage is a loan to buy a house, repaid with interest; a lease is an agreement to rent property for a time.
ww.An insurance policy that covers a tenant: Renters insurance covers belongings against loss; a lease is the contract between tenant and landlord and does not insure anything.
ww.A tax on property that owners pay to the: A property tax is charged to owners by a local government; a lease is a contract and is not a tax.

rw: A lease binds you for months or years, so reading it shows the rent amount, fees, rules on pets or guests, and how to end the agreement without penalty.

ww.To make the landlord friendlier, as read: Reading a lease will not make a landlord friendlier; its purpose is to understand your obligations and rights before you are legally bound.
ww.To avoid talking to the landlord about t: Reading the lease does not avoid talking with the landlord; if terms are unclear or unfair, you should ask questions or negotiate before signing.
ww.To make the document last longer once yo: A document does not last longer because you read it; reading helps you know your commitments, and the lease runs for its stated term.

rw: Reports such as Carfax list accidents, number of owners, mileage records and title problems like salvage or flood damage, helping you avoid costly surprises.

ww.Choosing a car's paint color before you: Paint color is visible to the eye and is not in a history report; the report shows records about the car's past.
ww.Paying for car repairs on the day that y: A report does not pay for repairs and is not for new cars; it provides information about a used car's past before you buy.
ww.Setting the price of new cars at the dea: Dealers and the market set prices; the history report only gives facts, though accidents or title problems in it can justify a lower offer.

rw: An independent mechanic can find hidden problems with the engine, brakes or frame that you might miss, and it gives you leverage to negotiate the price.

ww.Buy the first car that you see on the lo: Buying the first car you see skips comparison, and you may overpay or buy a car with problems; shopping around protects your wallet.
ww.Trust the seller's word and nothing else: Trusting only the seller is risky because sellers may overlook or hide defects; verify the car with a history report and an inspection.
ww.Skip the test drive before you pay the p: A test drive reveals handling, noises and comfort problems, so skipping it before paying could leave you with a car that has hidden issues.

rw: Total cost of ownership adds the purchase price to insurance, fuel, maintenance, repairs, taxes and depreciation, which often makes a cheap car more costly than expected.

ww.Only the sticker price shown on the wind: The sticker price is only the purchase price; owning a car also costs insurance, fuel, maintenance and repairs, so it understates the real cost.
ww.Only the monthly payment, the sole cost: Payments are only one part of owning a car; insurance, fuel, registration and repairs add to costs each year, so they are not the sole cost.
ww.Only the cost of gas that the car burns: Gas is just one cost of running a car; insurance, maintenance, repairs and the purchase price also count toward the total cost.

rw: The monthly cost is the payment plus running costs, so $200 + $150 = $350 per month for the car.

ww.$50: $50 is the difference between the two amounts ($200 - $150); the question asks for the total cost, so you add them.
ww.$200: $200 counts only the car payment and leaves out the $150 of insurance, fuel and upkeep that also come out every month.
ww.$150: $150 counts only the insurance, fuel and upkeep and leaves out the $200 payment, so it understates the monthly cost.

rw: Dining out daily is a want rather than a need, since you could cook at home, so cutting it frees up money for savings.

ww.Basic weekly groceries: Basic groceries are a need because people require food to live; you can cut costs by shopping smart, but groceries are not a want.
ww.Medicine for illness: Medicine for illness is a need tied to health and safety, so it is not something you should reduce to save money.
ww.Rent for your own home: Rent for your home is a need because everyone requires housing; you cannot simply cut it, though you might find a cheaper place.

rw: Originally $12 x 20 = $240, and after the cut $12 x 5 = $60, so the monthly savings are $240 - $60 = $180.

ww.$60: $60 is the cost of eating out 5 days ($12 x 5), which is the remaining spending, not the amount saved.
ww.$240: $240 is the original monthly spending ($12 x 20); the savings are the difference between that and the new cost of $60.
ww.$12: $12 is the cost of one day of dining out; the savings come from cutting 15 days, which is $12 x 15 = $180.

rw: A sinking fund collects small, regular amounts toward a known future cost, such as a vacation or car insurance bill, so you do not need debt.

ww.A fund that earns no interest at all for: A sinking fund is built with regular deposits and can earn interest in a savings account; earning nothing is not what defines it.
ww.A fund for emergencies only, not for pla: Emergency funds cover surprises; a sinking fund is for known, planned costs, such as a car repair or holiday gifts, so this is reversed.
ww.Money lost through bad investments and n: Money lost through bad investments is a loss, not a fund; a sinking fund is a deliberate savings plan for a future expense.

rw: Divide the goal by the months, so $1,200 / 12 = $100 a month, which gets you to the full trip budget by the date.

ww.$1,200: $1,200 is the total goal, not a monthly amount; saving it all in a single month would not spread the cost over the year.
ww.$10: $10 a month would raise only $120 in a year, one tenth of the goal; the monthly figure is $1,200 divided by 12.
ww.$12: $12 a month would raise only $144 in a year; to reach $1,200 in 12 months you need $100 each month.

rw: Keeping savings apart makes them less visible and harder to spend on impulse, which helps you reach goals such as an emergency fund.

ww.It makes the money tax free for all year: Keeping money in a separate account does not make it tax free; interest earned in a regular savings account is still taxable income.
ww.It removes the need to budget at all in: Separate accounts do not remove the need for a budget; you still need to plan spending and saving, and a separate account only supports that plan.
ww.It guarantees higher interest than any b: No account guarantees higher interest; rates depend on the bank and account type, and a separate account is about behavior rather than rate.

rw: Financial advisors suggest three to six months of essential costs, enough to cover rent, food and bills if income stops, with more for unstable income.

ww.No set amount is needed for any househol: Experts recommend a cushion for emergencies such as job loss or medical bills, so claiming no amount is needed is poor advice for any household.
ww.Ten years of expenses held in a savings: Ten years of expenses is far larger than the usual guideline and would tie up money that could be invested; most advice is three to six months.
ww.One day of expenses kept in a savings ac: One day of expenses would not cover a real emergency such as job loss, which can last weeks or months; the guideline is far larger.

rw: A three-month fund covers three months of essential costs, so $1,800 x 3 = $5,400 kept in an easily accessible savings account.

ww.$21,600: $21,600 is a full year of expenses ($1,800 x 12), which is much more than the three-month goal asked about.
ww.$600: $600 is one third of a single month's expenses ($1,800 / 3), which is not what a three-month fund requires.
ww.$1,800: $1,800 is only one month of essential expenses; a three-month fund requires multiplying that monthly amount by three, giving $5,400.

rw: When rates fall, savings accounts and maturing CDs reinvest at lower rates, so savers earn less income than before on new deposits.

ww.The risk that a bank fails and closes it: Bank failure is a separate risk, called institutional risk, and FDIC insurance covers deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, so it is not interest rate risk.
ww.The risk that you forget your PIN when y: Forgetting a PIN is an access inconvenience, not a financial risk related to rates; interest rate risk concerns the return you earn.
ww.The risk that prices rise and your money: That describes inflation risk, where rising prices erode purchasing power; interest rate risk is about changes in the rate your savings earn.

rw: Safe savings give stability and liquidity while diversified investments, like index funds, historically outpace inflation over decades, so a mix balances loss risk and inflation risk.

ww.All money in one risky stock that the in: A single stock concentrates risk; if the company fails, you can lose much of your savings, so it does not protect against loss.
ww.All cash under a mattress at home for th: Cash under a mattress earns no interest and loses buying power to inflation, and it can be lost or stolen, so it is unsafe.
ww.Spending it all now on whatever you feel: Spending everything now leaves no savings, so there is nothing to protect; it does not guard against loss or inflation in the future.

rw: An account you never opened may signal identity theft or a reporting mistake, and disputing it with the bureau protects your score and credit.

ww.Your correct name and address on the rep: Your correct name and address are accurate information, so there is nothing to dispute; disputes are for inaccurate or fraudulent items.
ww.A late payment that you really made last: A late payment you actually made late is accurate, so a dispute would not succeed; only inaccurate information can be removed.
ww.An account you opened and repaid in full: A properly closed, paid-off account is accurate and can even help your history; there is no error to dispute in it.

rw: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the bureau must investigate a dispute, usually within 30 days, and correct or delete items it cannot verify.

ww.Ignore the dispute and leave the report: The law requires bureaus to look into disputes, not ignore them; leaving the report unchanged without investigating would break the rules.
ww.Charge you a fee to look into the disput: Disputing errors is free; credit bureaus may not charge you to investigate a dispute about inaccurate information on your report.
ww.Raise your credit score by a set number: Bureaus fix errors but do not give bonus points; your score changes only if removing the error changes what the scoring model sees.

rw: A credit limit increase raises the maximum you may borrow on a card, and it can lower your utilization ratio if your balance stays the same.

ww.A new loan for the card's holder: A new loan is separate borrowed money with its own terms; a limit increase only changes how much you can charge on the existing card.
ww.A higher interest rate on the card: A higher interest rate raises the cost of carrying a balance; a limit increase raises the borrowing cap, which is not the same thing.
ww.A decrease in your balance owed there: A decrease in balance owed comes from making payments; a limit increase changes your borrowing ceiling and leaves the balance as it was.

rw: Before, $600 / $2,000 = 30%; after the increase, $600 / $3,000 = 20%, and lower utilization generally helps credit scores.

ww.It stays at 30% for good: Utilization is balance divided by limit, so when the limit changes and the balance stays the same, the ratio changes; it does not stay at 30%.
ww.It becomes zero at once: With a $600 balance on a $3,000 limit, utilization is 20%, not zero; it would be zero only if the balance were paid off.
ww.It rises from 30% to 40%: Utilization falls instead of rising: $600 / $3,000 = 20%, so a bigger limit lowers the ratio, which is not 40%.

rw: Paying only the minimum keeps most of the balance accruing interest, so repayment drags on for years and the total interest paid can exceed the original purchase.

ww.Never using the card, so that no interes: Never using the card avoids interest and is not a trap; the minimum payment trap occurs when you carry a balance and pay little each month.
ww.Paying the full balance so that no inter: Paying the full balance avoids interest through the grace period, which is the smart approach rather than a trap.
ww.Paying more than the minimum each month,: Paying more than the minimum clears debt faster and cuts interest, which is the way out of the trap, not the trap itself.

rw: Payments above the minimum go mostly toward principal, so the balance and the interest charged on it shrink faster, saving money.

ww.Skipping payments for a few months now: Skipping payments brings late fees, penalty rates and credit damage, and interest keeps adding to the balance, so it increases costs.
ww.Making new purchases on the card itself: New purchases add to the balance and interest charges, so this makes your debt larger instead of reducing interest costs.
ww.Paying only the minimum due every month: Minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the balance falls slowly and interest costs stay high compared with paying more.

rw: A personal loan lends a lump sum for needs like debt consolidation or medical bills, usually unsecured, repaid in fixed installments with interest.

ww.A loan only for businesses that is repai: Personal loans are available to individuals, not only businesses, and the equal installment feature does not make it a business-only loan.
ww.A tax refund paid by the state to a pers: A tax refund is money returned by the government, whereas a personal loan is borrowed money that must be repaid with interest.
ww.A gift from a bank to a customer that is: A bank never gives free money; a personal loan must be repaid with interest, typically in fixed monthly installments over a set term.

rw: Simple interest = $3,000 x 8% x 1 year = $240, which is the cost of borrowing before adding it to the principal.

ww.$2,400: $2,400 is eight times the real interest figure; simple interest is principal x rate x time = $3,000 x 0.08 x 1 = $240.
ww.$3,240: $3,240 is the total repaid, principal plus interest ($3,000 + $240), not the interest cost alone that the question asks for.
ww.$24: $24 results from misplacing a decimal; 8% of $3,000 is $240, so $24 is ten times too small.

rw: A home equity loan lets you borrow against the part of your home you own, but if you cannot repay, the lender can foreclose on the house.

ww.A grant given by the government to needy: A government grant is free money that need not be repaid; a home equity loan is borrowed money secured by your home and must be repaid.
ww.A loan for a car only, with the car as c: An auto loan uses the car as collateral; a home equity loan uses the owner's equity in their home as collateral.
ww.A loan with no collateral and no interes: Home equity loans have interest and collateral; they are not free, and the house secures the loan, which makes missing payments risky.

rw: A higher deductible means you pay more of the first costs, so the insurer pays out less often and charges a lower premium.

ww.It removes the insurer from your claims,: A deductible does not remove the insurer from claims; the insurer still pays covered costs above the deductible amount.
ww.It has no effect on premiums, since the: Deductibles do affect premiums; insurers offer lower premiums for higher deductibles because the policyholder shares more of the risk.
ww.It increases the insurer's risk, so prem: A higher deductible lowers the insurer's risk, so premiums go down; saying risk increases and premiums rise reverses the true relationship.

rw: Having an emergency fund means you can cover the deductible if a loss happens, so you can safely take the lower premium that goes with it.

ww.You have no savings at all to cover the: With no savings, a high deductible could be impossible to pay after a loss, so a lower deductible is safer.
ww.You expect to make many claims during th: If you expect many claims, a high deductible would make you pay out of pocket repeatedly, so a low deductible suits that situation better.
ww.You want the highest possible premium ev: Higher deductibles come with lower premiums, not the highest; wanting the highest premium would be a reason for a low deductible.

rw: Insurance fraud is knowingly lying or exaggerating to collect money, such as faking a theft or inflating a claim, and it is a crime with fines and jail.

ww.Filing an honest claim for a real loss t: Filing an honest claim for a real loss is the proper use of insurance and is not fraud, because there is no deception.
ww.Paying a premium late and getting a fee: Paying a premium late may bring a fee or a lapse in coverage, but it is a billing issue and not fraud.
ww.Comparing quotes from several firms to f: Comparing quotes is smart shopping and fully legal; it involves no lying or false claims, so it is not fraud.

rw: Claiming a sold car was stolen to collect money is a false claim, which is insurance fraud and can lead to criminal charges and a denied claim.

ww.Risk reduction: Risk reduction means lowering the chance or size of a loss, such as installing alarms; reporting a sold car stolen is deception.
ww.A legal claim: A legal claim is an honest request for payment on a real loss; this case involves a lie, so it is not a legal claim.
ww.Avoiding risk now: Avoiding risk means not doing an activity that could cause a loss; reporting a false theft is not risk avoidance but fraud.

rw: Replacement cost coverage pays what it costs to buy a new equivalent item today, without subtracting depreciation, though premiums are usually higher.

ww.A policy that pays only the item's depre: That describes actual cash value, which subtracts depreciation for age and wear; replacement cost pays the full current price instead.
ww.A policy that pays nothing at all for lo: A policy that pays nothing would be of no use; replacement cost policies pay out for covered losses at the current cost of replacing items.
ww.A policy that pays double the value of a: Policies pay up to the cost of replacing the item and never double it; paying double would let owners profit from a loss.

rw: Replacement cost pays up to the $900 needed to buy a new laptop, while actual cash value would pay only the $200 depreciated value.

ww.Actual cash value: Actual cash value pays the depreciated worth, about $200 for the old laptop, which is far less than the $900 for a new one.
ww.They pay the same: The two policy types pay differently here: ACV gives about $200 for the aged laptop, while replacement cost gives up to $900.
ww.Neither pays: Both policy types pay for a covered theft, so saying neither pays ignores that the laptop is stolen and covered in this case.

rw: A home inventory records items and their values, often with photos or receipts, so you can prove what you owned if you must make a claim.

ww.A tax record of what you owe each year t: A tax record of what you owe is a tax statement; a home inventory lists your belongings and values to support an insurance claim.
ww.A list of home repair tools kept in the: A list of tools kept in a shed covers just a few items; an insurance inventory covers all belongings, with values, photos and receipts.
ww.A bill from the insurer for your next pr: A premium bill is a request for payment from the insurer; a home inventory is a record you create of your own belongings.

rw: After a fire, an inventory proves what you owned and what it was worth, which speeds up the claim and helps you get a fair payout.

ww.It lowers the deductible on your policy: An inventory does not change your deductible, which is set in the policy; it only helps document the loss for your claim.
ww.It cancels your premium for the next yea: The inventory does not cancel premiums; you still owe premiums, and it only helps you document belongings for a claim.
ww.It prevents any future fire, as insurers: An inventory cannot prevent fires; it is a record made for documenting losses after the fact, and does not change fire risk.

rw: Accounts such as 401(k)s and IRAs may let contributions reduce taxable income now or let earnings grow tax-deferred or tax-free, increasing long-term growth.

ww.The account pays for your groceries, as: Retirement accounts do not pay for groceries; their tax advantage is about how contributions or earnings are taxed, not about spending money.
ww.No taxes ever apply to any account that: Taxes do apply to many bank accounts, as interest is taxable; retirement accounts are special because they offer tax breaks that others do not.
ww.Taxes are doubled on every dollar that y: Retirement accounts reduce taxes, not double them; the account gives a tax advantage, though early withdrawals can bring taxes and penalties.

rw: An employer match, such as 50 cents per dollar up to a limit, is an immediate return on your contribution, so skipping it means giving up part of your pay.

ww.It lowers your income tax to zero every: A match does not cut your tax to zero; pre-tax contributions may lower taxable income, but you still owe tax on the rest.
ww.It lets you withdraw anytime with no pen: Early withdrawals from a 401(k) generally bring a 10% penalty plus income tax, so a match does not allow penalty-free withdrawals anytime.
ww.It guarantees investment gains every sin: Investment returns are never guaranteed, and the match is a contribution from your employer, not a promise that investments will gain.
